questions.stem: A staff engineer wrote the team's TypeScript conventions (error handling, import order, no barrel files) into their `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Claude Code follows them on that engineer's laptop, but the other 59 engineers report that it ignores them. New hires must get the conventions automatically on their first day. What is the fix?

options.text: Move the conventions into the project CLAUDE.md (repo root or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`) and commit it.
options.why: Project memory travels with the repo, so every engineer, including new hires, gets it automatically.

options.text: Ship a bootstrap script in the repo that copies the conventions into each engineer's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` during onboarding.
options.why: This works on day one, but copies drift and every update needs re-running. User scope is the wrong layer.

options.text: Put the conventions in `.claude/settings.json`, which is the shared configuration Claude Code reads for team-wide behaviour.
options.why: Settings hold permissions, hooks and environment settings. Conventions belong in memory files.

options.text: Ask everyone to run `/memory` after pulling, so Claude Code re-indexes and loads the staff engineer's conventions.
options.why: `/memory` shows and edits memory files. It can't load a file that lives on someone else's machine.

questions.explanation: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is personal. Team conventions belong in project-scoped memory committed to the repo.

questions.stem: Testing conventions (fixture naming, no network calls, one `describe` per file) apply to every `*.test.ts` and `*.spec.tsx` file. There are about 1,100 such files spread across 40+ directories in `apps/` and `packages/`, and teams create new directories weekly. A previous attempt put the conventions in the root CLAUDE.md, but frontend engineers complained that Claude kept applying test rules while editing React components. Two teams then copied the section into their own directory CLAUDE.md files, and those copies have since diverged. The platform team wants the conventions applied automatically, only when relevant, with one file to maintain. What should they do?

options.text: Add a CLAUDE.md to each directory that holds tests, plus a CI check that fails when a new test directory lacks one.
options.why: This works, but it means 40+ copies to maintain, which violates the one-file requirement.

options.text: Add a "Testing" section to the root CLAUDE.md that begins "Apply only when editing test files".
options.why: One file, but it is always loaded and relies on inference to scope itself.

options.text: Create one `.claude/rules/testing.md` whose `paths:` frontmatter globs `**/*.test.ts` and `**/*.spec.tsx`.
options.why: One file, loaded automatically, and only for matching files wherever they live.

options.text: Create a `/testing-conventions` project skill and add a reminder to the PR template to invoke it.
options.why: One file, but not automatic, because it depends on someone invoking it.

questions.explanation: Each wrong option satisfies some of the constraints. Only a path-scoped rule satisfies all of them: automatic, scoped, and a single file.

questions.stem: The platform team wants every engineer to have a `/new-endpoint` command that scaffolds an API route following house conventions. They expect to revise it every few weeks, and want updates to reach everyone without anyone running a setup step. What is the best home for it?

options.text: Each engineer's `~/.claude/commands/`, populated by an onboarding script that engineers re-run whenever it changes.
options.why: Re-running a script is exactly the setup step the team wants to avoid.

options.text: An internal MCP server that exposes `new-endpoint` as a prompt to every connected Claude Code client.
options.why: Possible, but it means operating infrastructure for something a committed file does.

options.text: A `## Commands` section of the root CLAUDE.md that describes the steps and the trigger phrase `/new-endpoint`.
options.why: CLAUDE.md is memory. It doesn't define slash commands.

options.text: `.claude/commands/new-endpoint.md` in the repository, committed with the code.
options.why: Project commands update through git with no extra steps.

questions.explanation: Shared commands live in the project's `.claude/commands/`. Personal ones live in `~/.claude/commands/`.

questions.stem: The `/audit-deps` skill reads about 300 lockfile entries and dozens of changelogs, then writes a half-page risk report. Engineers like the report. But after running it, their sessions feel sluggish, and Claude forgets decisions made before the audit. The skill needs all the tools it currently uses. Which SKILL.md frontmatter change best fixes this?

options.text: Narrow `allowed-tools` to `Read` and `Grep`, so the skill can't run commands that produce large outputs.
options.why: The question says the skill needs its current tools, and the reads alone still flood the session.

options.text: Set `context: fork`, so the skill runs in an isolated context and only its report returns to the main session.
options.why: This isolates the verbose work while keeping the tools and the report.

options.text: Add an `argument-hint` asking for one package name, so engineers audit a single dependency at a time.
options.why: This changes the skill's purpose, since the full audit is what engineers value.

options.text: Add a final step to the skill body that runs `/compact`, shrinking the session once the report is written.
options.why: Compacting afterwards is lossy, which is how earlier decisions get forgotten.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` keeps a skill's verbose intermediate work out of the caller's context.

questions.stem: An engineer must migrate 120 files from a deprecated logging library. Two strategies are on the table. A thin adapter is quick and keeps the old API. A full call-site rewrite is cleaner but touches every file and changes log formats that two dashboards depend on. The tech lead wants the choice justified before any file changes. How should the engineer use Claude Code?

options.text: Direct execution with a prompt describing both strategies, letting Claude choose the better one as it works through the files.
options.why: The choice gets made implicitly and file by file, with no justification beforehand.

options.text: Plan mode to explore usage and the dashboard dependencies, settle and justify the strategy, then direct execution to migrate in batches.
options.why: Plan first, so the choice is justified as the tech lead asked, then execute.

options.text: An Explore subagent to catalogue call sites, after which the engineer writes a codemod without involving Claude in the decision.
options.why: Useful for discovery, but it skips the analysis that justifies the strategy.

options.text: Plan mode for the entire migration including the edits, so every change is reviewed against the plan as it is made.
options.why: Plan mode is for investigating and designing. The edits happen in execution.

questions.explanation: Plan mode suits large, multi-file work with an architectural choice. Direct execution then carries out the agreed plan.

questions.stem: An engineer asks Claude Code to rename a misspelled local variable (`recieved` → `received`) inside a single 30-line function in `apps/api/src/orders/sync.ts`. The variable isn't exported, and the engineer has already confirmed that it isn't used anywhere else. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Plan mode first, so Claude can confirm there are no other occurrences before changing anything.
options.why: The engineer has already confirmed that, so planning adds nothing.

options.text: An Explore subagent to map references, followed by direct execution using the subagent's findings.
options.why: This is unnecessary indirection for a confirmed local change.

options.text: Direct execution, because the change is local, small and fully specified.
options.why: Planning overhead isn't justified for a trivial, clear edit.

options.text: A forked session, so the rename is easy to discard if something unexpected breaks.
options.why: Version control already provides that, so a fork adds nothing.

questions.explanation: Match the mode to the task: well-scoped, small changes go straight to execution.

questions.stem: Claude Code keeps suggesting `moment.js`, which the team banned a month ago. The ban is documented in the root CLAUDE.md. The engineer suspects an older memory file, perhaps an imported one or one in a parent directory, still recommends it. They want to find and fix the source within a few minutes. What should they do?

options.text: Search the repo and home directory for every CLAUDE.md file and open each one, looking for moment.js references.
options.why: This is slow and misses imported files and other memory sources.

options.text: Run `/memory` to see which memory files are loaded, then open and edit the offending one.
options.why: This is the built-in way to inspect the memory files actually in effect, including imported ones.

options.text: Start Claude Code with debug logging and read the startup output to see which files were parsed.
options.why: Indirect and noisy. The built-in command answers the question directly.

options.text: Add a stronger ban to the root CLAUDE.md in capitals, so it outweighs whatever older instruction exists.
options.why: This leaves the conflicting instruction in place and hopes the stronger wording wins.

questions.explanation: `/memory` shows the loaded memory hierarchy and lets you edit it directly.

questions.stem: The root CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines: API style, Terraform rules, frontend patterns, release steps and on-call notes. Engineers report that instructions in the middle are often ignored. Frontend engineers also complain that Terraform rules show up in their sessions. What is the best restructuring?

options.text: Rewrite the file as terse bullet points without examples, cutting it to about 300 lines while keeping one file.
options.why: Shorter helps, but Terraform rules still load for frontend engineers, and dropping the examples costs quality.

options.text: Move the most-ignored sections to the top and bottom of the file, where the model attends most reliably.
options.why: This works around lost-in-the-middle but ignores the relevance complaint.

options.text: Turn each section into a skill, so only the relevant conventions load when an engineer invokes them.
options.why: Always-needed conventions would then depend on someone remembering to invoke a skill.

options.text: Keep shared essentials in CLAUDE.md with `@` imports, and move area conventions to `.claude/rules/` or subdirectory CLAUDE.md files.
options.why: This solves both complaints: less always-loaded content, and conventions that load where they're relevant.

questions.explanation: Use `@import`, `.claude/rules/` and directory-level memory for modular CLAUDE.md organisation.

questions.stem: Claude has produced three versions of a `formatFiscalWeek()` helper. Each one mishandles different edge cases: fiscal years starting in February, ISO week 53, and users in UTC−10. The requirements are two paragraphs of prose that the product manager wrote, and both Claude and the engineer now interpret them differently. What is the most effective next step?

options.text: Give 2–3 concrete input/output examples or failing tests for the edge cases, then iterate until they pass.
options.why: Concrete cases resolve the ambiguity in the prose, which is the root problem.

options.text: Rewrite the prose using RFC-style MUST/SHOULD language and ask Claude to re-read it carefully before coding.
options.why: More formal prose can still be read two ways. Examples pin the meaning down.

options.text: Turn on extended thinking, so Claude reasons through every edge case implied by the current description.
options.why: More reasoning over an ambiguous specification doesn't reveal what was intended.

options.text: Ask Claude for five alternative implementations and pick whichever looks closest to the product manager's intent.
options.why: This gives choice without a criterion. Tests supply the criterion.

questions.explanation: Iterate against concrete examples and tests. The interview pattern also helps when the requirements are ambiguous.

questions.stem: After two hours exploring the billing module, Claude's answers are vaguer, and it has contradicted two conclusions it confirmed an hour earlier: which service owns invoice numbering, and where proration happens. The engineer still needs to implement a change that depends on both. What should they do?

options.text: Keep going, but restate the two confirmed conclusions at the start of each new prompt so they stay near the end of the context.
options.why: This patches the two known facts, but the degraded context remains and will drop others.

options.text: Write the confirmed findings to a notes file (or run `/compact`), then continue from the summary or in a fresh session.
options.why: Persisting findings and resetting the context directly counters long-session degradation.

options.text: Paste the billing module source into the chat again, so Claude reasons from complete, fresh information.
options.why: More bloat makes the degradation worse.

options.text: Switch to a model with a larger context window and replay the session, so nothing from the exploration is lost.
options.why: This is costly, and a larger window doesn't stop attention from diluting over a long session.

questions.explanation: Persist findings, compact or summarise, and continue in a fresh context.

questions.stem: Before changing the auth flow, an engineer wants a survey of how 30 services call the auth library: which functions, which options and any wrappers. The main session already holds important design decisions from the morning, and grep output for the library runs to about 4,000 lines. What is the best approach?

options.text: Run the searches in the main session but tell Claude to keep only a running summary, ignoring the raw output.
options.why: The raw output still lands in the main context.

options.text: Delegate the survey to a subagent such as Explore, which works in its own context and returns a concise structured summary.
options.why: This isolates the 4,000 lines of discovery and protects the morning's decisions.

options.text: Run the survey in the main session, then `/compact` before starting the auth change itself.
options.why: This works, but it risks the morning's decisions in the lossy compaction.

options.text: Have Claude read the auth library's source and infer how services are likely to call it.
options.why: Inference isn't a survey, and it will miss wrappers and real usage.

questions.explanation: Use subagents for verbose exploration so the main session keeps its essential context.

questions.stem: Yesterday an engineer worked on a feature in a named session, `orders-v2`. Overnight a teammate merged a refactor that renamed `OrderService` to `OrderCoordinator`, moved four functions into new files, and changed two of the signatures the feature depends on. The engineer wants to continue efficiently. What should they do?

options.text: Resume `orders-v2` and continue, since Claude Code notices that files have changed and re-reads them automatically.
options.why: Claude would reason from the stale file contents still in its history.

options.text: Fork `orders-v2` so yesterday's state is preserved, and continue the feature in the fork.
options.why: A fork inherits the same stale context.

options.text: Rebase the feature branch onto the pre-refactor commit, so the files match the session's view.
options.why: This works against merged team work and only postpones the conflict.

options.text: Start fresh with a structured summary of yesterday's decisions, or resume and tell Claude exactly what changed so it re-reads those files.
options.why: Either option replaces the stale context with current information.

questions.explanation: After significant external changes, tell a resumed session what changed, or start fresh with a summary.

questions.stem: After 40 minutes analysing the caching layer, an engineer wants to compare two implementations, write-through and write-behind, starting from that same analysis. Each attempt should see none of the other's reasoning, so the comparison is fair. What should they do?

options.text: Fork the session (`--fork-session` with `--resume`, or `fork_session` in the SDK) and run each attempt in its own branch.
options.why: Both branches share the analysis and stay independent of each other.

options.text: Try write-through first, run `/compact`, then try write-behind in the same session using the compacted history.
options.why: The compacted summary still carries the first attempt's reasoning into the second.

options.text: Open a brand-new session for the second attempt and paste in a summary of the 40-minute analysis.
options.why: This works, but the summary loses detail, so the two attempts don't start from the same point.

options.text: Use plan mode for one attempt and direct execution for the other, which keeps their reasoning separate.
options.why: Modes don't isolate context.

questions.explanation: Session forking explores alternatives from a common baseline.

questions.stem: Every engineer's Claude Code should connect to the company's issue-tracker MCP server. Each engineer has a personal API token, because the tracker records who made each change. Security forbids committing secrets, and the platform team wants the server definition version-controlled. How should this be configured?

options.text: Each engineer adds the server and their token to user-level `~/.claude.json`, following a wiki setup page.
options.why: Tokens stay private, but the server definition isn't version-controlled.

options.text: Commit `.mcp.json` with a read-only service-account token, so a leak has limited impact.
options.why: This commits a secret, and it loses per-user attribution.

options.text: Commit a project `.mcp.json` that defines the server and references `${TRACKER_TOKEN}`, which each engineer sets locally.
options.why: This meets all three constraints: version-controlled, no committed secret, and per-user attribution.

options.text: Put the server URL in CLAUDE.md and have Claude ask each engineer for their token at the start of every session.
options.why: CLAUDE.md isn't MCP configuration, and tokens typed into chat end up in transcripts.

questions.explanation: Project-scope `.mcp.json` plus `${ENV_VAR}` expansion gives shared configuration with per-user secrets.

questions.stem: A modernisation spanning 14 phases and about 400 files has been interrupted twice this week, once by a laptop crash and once by an automatic compaction. Each time, Claude redid some finished files and skipped others it believed were done. Which TWO practices make this work reliably resumable? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A manifest file listing each file or phase with its status, which Claude updates as it works and reads on restart.
options.why: Progress becomes durable outside the context window.

options.text: A short notes file summarising each completed phase, written before the next phase begins.
options.why: Phase summaries carry the essential state forward compactly.

options.text: Relying on `--resume` after a crash, since it restores the full conversation, including what was done.
options.why: The conversation isn't a reliable progress ledger, and it may hold stale state.

options.text: Raising the output token limit, so Claude processes bigger batches and finishes before compaction is needed.
options.why: Output limits don't govern context growth or crash recovery.

options.text: Committing to git after every file, so the commit history itself shows which files are already migrated.
options.why: Helpful for safety, but inferring status from commit history is indirect and error-prone without an explicit ledger.

questions.explanation: Durable external state (manifests, notes) plus phase summaries make long-running work robust.

questions.stem: The team shares a `/review` skill in `.claude/skills/review/`. One senior engineer prefers a much more verbose variant that explains the reasoning behind every suggestion. The rest of the team explicitly voted to keep the shared skill concise. How should the engineer get the variant?

options.text: Add a `--verbose` argument to the shared skill and commit it, so anyone can opt in to the detailed behaviour.
options.why: Reasonable in general, but it changes the shared asset that the team voted to keep as is.

options.text: Create a personal skill under a different name, such as `review-verbose`, in `~/.claude/skills/`.
options.why: The variant is personal, uses a distinct name, and leaves the shared skill untouched.

options.text: Create a personal skill with the same name, `review`, in `~/.claude/skills/`, so it overrides the team version locally.
options.why: A clashing name makes it ambiguous which skill runs.

options.text: Add "when I run /review, explain every suggestion" to the project's root CLAUDE.md file.
options.why: This changes behaviour for the whole team and adds always-loaded content.

questions.explanation: Keep personal variations in user scope under distinct names. Project scope is for shared team assets.
